title: RNA synthesis and substrate analogue inhibition in the CCHFV polymerase.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Searched the Protein Data Bank (PDB, the public archive of 3D molecular structures) by this paper's DOI: it returns exactly 4 entries (25XL, 25XM, 25XN, 25XO), released 2026-08-05, all cryo-electron microscopy at 2.67-3.18 Angstrom. I downloaded 25XN.cif (2.77 MB) and parsed it: one 3,094-residue protein chain (the viral L protein), five short RNA/peptide chains of 4-13 residues, and manganese and zinc ions. Europe PMC returns no data links, no supplementary files and no full text for this paper.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract's claims that minigenome replication assays (a cell-based test of viral RNA copying) support the structural interaction networks, and that nucleotide analogues with the same ribose 2'-modification as the hepatitis C drug sofosbuvir cause immediate chain termination. I never saw those numbers: the paper is closed access (Europe PMC isOpenAccess = N, no PMCID), so the Extended Data and Source Data tables holding the mutant activities and inhibition potencies are behind the publisher paywall.

a1_downloadable.note: Partly. The 4 structures and 4 maps download freely with no login (I fetched 25XN.cif successfully). But the quantitative assay data - mutant replication activities and inhibitor potencies - is only in the paywalled article's Source Data, which Europe PMC cannot serve. The structures alone pass A1; the measurements I would actually want to predict do not.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no label column anywhere in the downloadable data. The PDB/EMDB deposition is coordinate files and density maps only - no activity, potency or phenotype table. Any prediction target (replication activity per mutant, inhibition potency per analogue) would have to be hand-transcribed out of paywalled figures, which is exactly the 'construct the label yourself' failure A2 names.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not reached in the checklist order, but recorded: the L protein sequence and the bound RNA sequences are present inside the mmCIF files, so inputs would not need external lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Not reached. No measurement table exists in the open data, so there is nothing for units to be stated on. Inhibition potencies in the paper are presumably in micromolar or as IC50 (half-maximal inhibitory concentration), but I could not see them.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified by PDB DOI search: 4 structures total. Even counting the unseen assay data generously, targeted mutagenesis in a structural paper is typically tens of point mutants and a handful of nucleotide analogues - two to three orders of magnitude under the ~1,500-row bar (or ~400 for classification). This is the decisive failure.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~11 MB for four mmCIF coordinate files; cryo-EM maps add a few hundred MB if wanted
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized. Not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The abstract's '3.0 Angstrom resolution polymerase elongation complex' matches entry 25XN at 3.01 Angstrom, and the ~4,000-residue L protein matches the 3,094 modelled residues in chain A (the rest being disordered). No discrepancy found.

a8_label_provenance.note: Not reached. No label exists to trace. Note for the record that cryo-EM atomic coordinates are themselves a model fitted to a density map, so using them as a prediction target would be the circularity A8 warns about.

c2_audit.note: Not searched: the evaluation stopped at the Part A failure (A2 and A5). The empty list does not mean no models exist - viral polymerase inhibitor prediction is in fact an active area.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with four structures and no measurement table, nothing can be trained or tested.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use viral polymerase structure and nucleotide analogue chemistry to predict which analogues stop the virus copying its genome.
plain_idea.train_on: What the model would see: the 3D structure of the Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus L protein active site (the enzyme that copies the viral genome) together with the chemical structure of a candidate nucleotide analogue drug. Verified example count from this paper: 4 structures and an unknown, certainly small, number of tested analogues.
plain_idea.predict: Whether and how strongly each analogue blocks RNA synthesis, measured in the paper by biochemical polymerase assays and cell-based minigenome replication assays. I could not open those measurements, so I cannot confirm their format or units.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups developing antivirals for Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, a tick-borne disease with no approved drug, would use a reliable potency predictor to choose which analogues to synthesise. But this paper supplies far too few measured examples to build one.

ml_idea: The only machine-learning idea this paper supports is to use its elongation-complex structures as input features for a model trained mostly on other data - for example, adding the CCHFV polymerase to a cross-viral nucleotide-analogue potency model assembled from ChEMBL or published antiviral screens. That makes this paper a source of 4 structural features, not a training set, so it is not a project on its own.

effort.compute_note: Only the four mmCIF files are open; I measured 25XN at 2.77 MB and extrapolated the rest. No modelling cost estimated because there is no training set to run cross-validation on.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Search the PDB by this paper's DOI and count the entries. It returns 4. That single query, which took under a minute, kills the project.

verdict_reason: This is a cryo-electron microscopy structure paper, and its entire open dataset is 4 atomic structures plus 4 density maps, which I verified by searching the Protein Data Bank on the DOI and by downloading and parsing 25XN.cif. A5 (enough rows) fails by orders of magnitude: 4 examples against a ~1,500-row bar. A2 fails too, because the downloadable files contain coordinates only - the replication-assay activities and nucleotide-analogue potencies that would be the prediction target live in the paywalled article's Source Data, so the label would have to be transcribed by hand from figures I cannot access. The biology is important (no approved drug exists for Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever) and the structures are genuinely useful as input features for a model trained on other data, but there is no training set here.
